catalog_quote: An example is Tahitian, as discussed in Tyron (1976), Vergnaud and Halle (1978). The stress pattern of this language is as follows: (3) a. Stress the leftmost long vowel or vowel cluster. b. Otherwise stress the penult. As Tyron states that vowel clusters in Tahitian are tautosyllabic, this stress pattern can be expressed very simply in the following way: (4) a. On the [+syl] projection, form a right dominant, unbounded foot, labeling dominant nodes as strong iff they branch. b. Form a left dominant word tree. Some examples are: ... tamaaroa "boy" ... pahii "ship" ... ?ohipa "work" ... fare "house" ... The crucial cases here are (5)e and f. Because these words contain no long vowels, they are encompassed in a single foot; and since the dominant node of this foot doesn't branch, stress falls on the penult. sweep_summary: Tahitian (tahi1242) is in the catalog as classification weight on Hayes 1980's restatement of Tryon. Two title-hits: (1) Vergnaud & Halle 1978 'Metrical Structures in Phonology' is an unpublished MIT manuscript (Glottolog 5.3 record read; Hayes 1980 cites it as 'unpublished manuscript, MIT') with no digital copy anywhere I could find -- low priority, its Tahitian content is the same Tryon description Hayes already restates. (2) Bickmore 1995 'Refining and Formalizing the Tahitian Stress Placement Algorithm' (Oceanic Linguistics 34(2):410-442, DOI 10.2307/3623050) is the dedicated study and is paywalled (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/S2 all closed; JSTOR, MUSE, HathiTrust, CORE, BASE, Scholar blocked) -- high priority; online with a university library loginexists per. Second-hand reads of it: Zuraw 2018 sec. 6.3 (held) quotes Bickmore 1995:412-413 data showing penultimate default with stressed long/rising-VV penults (confirms weight-sensitivity); the Wikipedia article (rev 1372600686) summarizes Bickmore pp.417-435 as a right-edge three-syllable window with secondary stress on heavy syllables and final-syllable extrametricality in V1ʔV1 words, which would refine/partly contradict the unbounded 'leftmost long vowel' clause. New this search of works with stress in the title: downloaded the open ANU copy of the primary, Tryon 1970 Conversational Tahitian (hdl 1885/114918), and read §8 'Stress' pp.5-6 first-hand -- its four rules (stress the long vowel / first vowel of a vowel sequence; the first such sequence if two; else penult; each compound member stressed) match the catalog quote exactly, so classification weight is confirmed by the primary and the catalog's cite/loc can now point at Tryon 1970:5-6 instead of 'primary not reachable'. Also re-downloaded Hayes 1980 from MIT DSpace and verified the deciding quotation at printed pp.175-176.

new_statements.quote: there are four stress rules which are in evidence: (i) In words containing either a sequence of different vowels or a long vowel, the stress falls on the first vowel of the sequence, or on the long vowel. [...] (ii) With words containing two such sequences (i.e. sequences of different or same vowels, that is, long vowels), then the stress falls on the first of the sequences in the word. [...] (iii) With words not containing long vowels or sequences of vowels, the stress falls on the penultimate syllable. [...] (iv) With compound words, usually polysyllabic, each part of the compound takes its own stress.
new_statements.citation: Tryon, D. T. 1970. Conversational Tahitian: an introduction to the Tahitian language of French Polynesia. Canberra: Australian National University Press (open-access digitisation, ANU Open Research hdl 1885/114918). Section 8 'Stress', pp. 5-6.
new_statements.reading: First-hand primary statement (pedagogical grammar, 1970). Tahitian word stress is weight-sensitive: a long vowel or a vowel sequence attracts stress (on the long vowel / on the first vowel of the sequence, e.g. tiare, pahī, tamaiti); when a word has two such sequences the first (leftmost) one is stressed (tamāroa, farāoa); words with neither get penultimate stress (fare, ma'o, 'ohipa); each member of a compound keeps its own stress. Tryon also notes (p.2 fn) that a long vowel is treated as a sequence of two identical vowels for §§7-8. This is exactly the description Hayes 1980 pp.175-176 formalizes as '(3)a. Stress the leftmost long vowel or vowel cluster. b. Otherwise stress the penult.' -- so the catalog's classification weight is confirmed by the primary. Caveat: Bickmore 1995 (not read; paywalled) reportedly bounds stress to the final three syllables and adds secondary stress on heavy syllables, which would refine Tryon's unbounded rule (ii).

audit.recode_to: Keep classification weight (CVV heavy; no codas) -- Bickmore's system as reported is still quantity-sensitive. On reading Bickmore 1995: expect the primary-stress rule -> 'penult by default; final syllable if it contains a long vowel or diphthong; antepenult if it has a long vowel and the penult is light (right-edge three-syllable window)'; edge 'unclear' -> right; the secondary-stress rule 'none described' -> secondary stress on heavy syllables and on non-final members of compounds/reduplicants. Also update cite/loc to point at the held primary Tryon 1970:6 (ANU hdl 1885/114918) instead of 'primary not reachable', and grade from quotation carried over second-hand from StressTyp2 to primary-confirmed for the Tryon statement.

sources.quote: TAHITIAN. Tahitian, which also has penultimate stress, tolerates HL# even more than Nukuoro, with no variation reported. Stress simply falls on a long penult vowel, including in loans, as illustrated in 42a. Sequences like ae, ao, au also draw stress onto the /a/ (as in 42b). [...] (42) Tahitian heavy penults a. stressed, long penult (Bickmore 1995:412): váahi 'place', máaha 'satisfied', péeni 'paint' (loan), faráani 'French' (loan); short penult for contrast: túpu, mána, póto, ferúri. b. rising vowel sequences (Bickmore 1995:413): Ɂáeto 'eagle', faráoa 'flour' (loan), táura 'rope' [Zuraw 2018 reporting Bickmore, not Bickmore's own text]

sources.note: The only dedicated study of Tahitian stress; second-hand reports (Walker 1997 fn.10, held) say it replaces the Tryon/Hayes unbounded 'leftmost heavy, else penult' rule our the primary-stress rule quotes with a right-edge three-syllable window (penult default, final if heavy, antepenult if long V + light penult) and adds secondary stress on heavy syllables -- would fix our edge='unclear' and the secondary-stress rule='none described'.
